name: Handing someone their data back, or deleting it
summary: When a person asks for a copy of their data or asks you to erase it, you can do both — and prove you did.

provenance.source: SimpleHire — its GDPR export and deletion services, including the hard lesson that tables not reachable by a database cascade have to be listed by hand or they survive the deletion
provenance.changes: Generalised away from its domain tables into a registry the project fills in, so that adding a table forces a decision about what happens to it on erasure.

env.name: DATA_RETENTION_DAYS
env.description: How long you keep records before deleting them automatically.

extensionPoints.description: List every table holding personal data and say what happens to it on erasure.

postInstall: Fill in the registry with every table that holds personal data. A table left out is one that survives an erasure request.
Write down how long you keep data and why. Shipyard asks for this before you go live.
limitations: It deletes from your database. Copies in backups, in your email provider, in your analytics or in a spreadsheet on somebody's laptop are not touched.
The registry is filled in by you. Nothing can detect a table you forgot to list.
Whether your handling satisfies the law where you operate is a question for a lawyer, not this component.
solves: let someone download all their data
delete a person's data when they ask
